title: Daily sodium guideline
text: The FDA Daily Value for sodium is less than 2,300 mg a day — a general reference value based on a 2,000-calorie diet, not a personal target. That's about one teaspoon of salt total from all food and drink combined, not just what you add. On packaged food labels, 5% Daily Value (DV) or less per serving is a 'low' amount of sodium and 20% DV or more is 'high'. Most sodium in a typical U.S. diet comes from packaged, restaurant, and dining-hall foods rather than the salt shaker — the practical move is to compare labels at the store and ask for sauce or dressing on the side when eating out.
source: FDA Nutrition Facts label education; Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025 (sodium)

title: Daily fiber guideline
text: The FDA Daily Value for fiber is at least 28 grams a day — a general reference value based on a 2,000-calorie diet, not a personal target. Most college-aged adults get about half that. Easy ways to close the gap: a cup of oats or a slice of 100% whole-grain bread at breakfast (about 4–5 g each), a cup of beans or lentils with a meal (about 7–10 g), a piece of fruit for a snack (2–4 g), and vegetables at lunch and dinner.
source: FDA Nutrition Facts label (Daily Values); Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025

title: Daily fruit and vegetable guideline
text: The Dietary Guidelines for Americans suggest about 2 cups of fruit and 2½ cups of vegetables per day for most college-aged adults — slightly more or less depending on activity level. Whole fruit counts fully; 100% juice counts once (about 1 cup max). Dark leafy greens, red/orange vegetables, and beans/peas are the ones that most people fall short on. Frozen and canned (rinsed) count — fresh isn't a requirement.
source: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025, Chapter 1 and MyPlate

title: Daily whole grain guideline
text: The Dietary Guidelines recommend making at least HALF of your grains whole. On packaged food labels, look for 'whole wheat' or 'whole grain' as the first ingredient — not just 'wheat flour' or 'enriched flour'. In a dining hall, swapping white rice for brown rice, or white bread for 100% whole-wheat, is the single easiest move.
source: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025, Chapter 1 and MyPlate (grains)

title: Daily added sugars guideline
text: The FDA Daily Value for added sugars is less than 50 g (12 teaspoons) a day — a general reference value based on a 2,000-calorie diet, not a personal target. The biggest source for most college-aged adults is sugar-sweetened drinks (soda, sweet tea, flavored coffees, energy drinks, specialty lattes). A 12 oz can of regular soda has about 39 g — close to a full day's worth in one drink. On labels, look for 10% DV or less for added sugars per serving.
source: FDA Nutrition Facts label (added sugars); Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025

title: Daily saturated fat guideline
text: The FDA Daily Value for saturated fat is less than 20 g a day — a general reference value based on a 2,000-calorie diet, not a personal target. Big sources: fatty meats, butter, full-fat cheese and ice cream, and most fried fast food. Swaps that stack up: fish or beans in place of a fatty meat a couple of nights a week; olive oil in place of butter when cooking; a thinner layer of cheese on sandwiches.
source: FDA Nutrition Facts label (saturated fat); Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025

title: How to read a Nutrition Facts label in 15 seconds
text: A fast way to read any Nutrition Facts label: (1) Serving size first — the whole package often holds 2 or 3 servings. (2) Scan 'Added sugars', 'Saturated fat', and 'Sodium' — 5% Daily Value or less is 'low', 20% DV or more is 'high'. (3) Scan 'Fiber' — 20% DV or more per serving is 'high' and generally helpful. When comparing two products, lower sat fat, lower sodium, lower added sugars, and higher fiber per serving are the four to watch.

title: Calorie-counting and weight questions in LLHS
text: LLHS is a habit-based program — not something that works with calorie counts or body-size targets. If a student asks about calorie amounts or body-size change, respond with a short, supportive sentence that reframes toward the habit (what to add, build, swap, or try), and suggest reaching out to the study team or a dietitian for the specifics.

title: When the planned food option isn't available
text: If the option in your plan isn't available, pick the closest thing on offer — a better choice still counts even when it's not the one you wrote down. The three usual swaps: (1) if a whole-grain option is missing, pick the dish with vegetables or beans on it instead; (2) if a fish entrée is missing, grab beans or a lean grilled option; (3) if a lower-sodium side is missing, add a piece of fruit or a side salad to balance a saltier main. Save the actual plan for the next day it IS available.
source: LLHS coping strategies (based on Week 2 planning spec)
